Tide Lines review: From Park Bar to OVO Hydro, the band comes full circle
21st September
Trad music
Entertainment
Music
Scotland
By
Laura Pollock
Digital Audience and Content Editor
Share
0 comments
Tide Lines at the OVO Hydro (Image: Laura Pollock)
This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today,
and has been written by our American colleagues.
It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald.
TIDE Lines' tenth anniversary celebrations saw them play their biggest headline show yet at the OVO Hydro on Saturday night.
Marking ten years since the release of their debut single Far Side of the World, the foursome took to the stage, proclaiming how much it meant to play the show in Glasgow.
“All four of us have stood out there and sat up there and watched all our favourite bands in the world play on this stage here,” frontman Robert Robertson – from Lochaber – told the crowd.
“So, it's a real privilege to be here tonight playing for you.”
With Robertson and keyboard player Ross Wilson – from the Isle of Mull – first performing together at the iconic Park Bar just a short walk from the venue, the band’s journey really is a story of solid graft in the big city.
READ MORE: Calvin Harris breaks world record after playing to 1.6m people
In a decade, the band known for their youthful trad takes have carved out one of the UK’s biggest independent success stories. They have earned four consecutive Scottish number 1 albums and UK top 15 chart successes, going from playing village halls and grassroots venues to selling tens of thousands of tickets across the country and Europe.
Saturday night was for the core fanbase. Dozens had been bussed from the Park Bar to support the boys who made it their home when they first moved to the city, arriving wearing their kilts and bows in their hair for the celebration.
Drummer Gus Munro (Glasgow) and guitarist Ali Turner (Alness) – also on the bagpipes – had completed the ensemble, meeting Robertson and Wilson through the Glasgow trad scene, to make Tide Lines.
The four of them performed for the very first time as a band at Tiree Music Festival back in 2016. I had been at the festival this year to see them return and have that full circle moment, and so with the experience of seeing the crowd there, I was intrigued to see them hold the attention of the Hydro.
The set list was almost a chronological retelling of their journey, from the early hits featuring the tales of the Hebridean breeze to some from their 2025 album Glasgow Love Story – a tribute to the city “that set them on their path”, they said.
Tide Lines at the OVO Hydro (Image: Laura Pollock)
All these visuals were all part of the show taking you across waves, over contour lines on Highland maps, along the Clyde skyline and through the streets of Glasgow.
Introducing Wild Mountain Thyme, Robertson said: “This next one's an old traditional song.
“It was one of the first songs that myself and Ross ever played together, and our first ever gig, the two of us in a bar very near here, a place called the Park Bar – when we didn’t have any songs of our own.
“We thought we would dust it off tonight. And that maybe you guys could all join in with us.”
This was the only cover by the band in a real tribute to their former selves. Outwith Wild Mountain Thyme, they were constantly taking their earpieces out to hear the crowd sing back their lyrics from over the years, beaming from ear to ear.
READ MORE: Lorraine Kelly leads outcry over St Andrews University 'anti-Scottish classism' row
Robertson is the main songwriter and singer, writing the lyrics and melody with guitar chords, before his bandmates flesh the tunes out. His voice could be considered one of the most powerful in the Scottish trad scene, and is instantly recognisable.
Munro wielded incredibly power from behind the drumkit, and this palpable electricity was elevated when Turner picked up his bagpipes.
The silhouette of Turner picking up the instrument triggered an intake of breath from those standing around me. Throughout, he held the audience in the palm of his hand and following his solo, I heard the words “that was insane” from behind.
Unbeknown to us, his solo was a distraction while Robertson ran round to the back of the standing crowd to use a B-stage. The others joined him “to really savour” the Hydro crowd.
A phenomenal visual followed of the four of them, from my perspective near the main stage, surrounded by a sea of phone torches and appearing small – but so elevated by their fans.
Tide Lines at the OVO Hydro (Image: Laura Pollock)
While their chart success is formidable, Tide Lines showed on Saturday night that their biggest achievement isn’t the charts or the trophies – it’s the community they’ve built from the Park Bar to the Hydro.
While it wasn't quite a Tiree-level experience – potentially due to the lack of familiarity on a stage on that scale – they did deliver a party for fans to remember.
The four concluded the evening with smiles as anniversary confetti rained down on them and us, and I would guess, there were a few tears back stage after that rollercoaster of nostalgia.
